title: Slack AI prompt injection can leak data from private channels
summary: Researchers showed that a message posted in a public Slack channel could carry instructions that Slack AI follows when another user later asks it a question. In the demonstration, Slack AI answered a user's request for a secret kept in a private channel with a fake re-authentication link that carried the secret to the attacker's server. A product change on 14 August 2024 also brought files from channels and DMs into Slack AI answers, widening the exposure. Slack initially described the behaviour as intended; Salesforce later said it had deployed a patch and had no evidence of unauthorized access to customer data. The researchers and the vendor disagree on whether the attacker needed an account in the same workspace.
attack_vector: Indirect prompt injection: attacker-written channel content retrieved into the assistant's context and followed as instructions, exfiltrating data through a rendered link
root_cause: The assistant combined content the user may not trust (public-channel messages) with private data in one context and rendered model-generated links
impact: Secrets and other content from private channels could be exfiltrated without the attacker having access to those channels
source: Researchers' disclosure and press coverage including the vendor's statement
